events.excerpt: Description A few small nit cleanups on the synchronizer component in consensus. Behavior change: fetch_blocks_from_peers now returns as soon as no request is in flight, instead of idling until the 4s FETCH_FROM_PEERS_TIMEOUT. This affects two cases: no request was sent because every selected block was already locked, or the last outstanding request failed with no peer left to retry on. In both cases no further network request is sent, and a failed request still waits the full 2s request timeout, so periodic runs cannot repeat faster than every ~2s on failures. The only new cost is local: while all selected blocks are locked, the scheduler polls get_missing_blocks at its default 200ms cadence instead of every 4s, which is the same cadence it already uses during fast successful sync. Added a test covering both cases. Test plan CI/PT Release notes Check each box that your changes affect. If none of the boxes relate to your changes, release notes aren't required. events.excerpt: Summary This proposal introduces post-quantum signature aggregation with leanVM in shadow mode . BLS remains the only authority for aggregates: consensus validity depends on BLS alone, exactly as today. leanVM aggregates and proofs are produced and verified alongside BLS, but their results have no effect on consensus. They are only measured, compared, and reported. When PQ/AI day arrives, an emergency hard fork simply retires BLS and enables leanVM in full. By “PQ/AI day” we mean the point at which quantum computers, or AI-assisted cryptanalysis, make BLS unsafe to rely on. Motivation Ethereum has to be ready for post-quantum signatures well before BLS is actually broken. Waiting until the last moment would mean deploying new, complex code to mainnet in a hurry. Giving leanVM authority early has its own risk: leanVM is new code that hasn’t been tested in production. However carefully it is built and audited, we can’t rule out a soundness bug that accepts an invalid proof, or a liveness bug that rejects a valid one. The main benefit of shadow mode is that Ethereum isn’t put at risk from a leanVM bug before PQ/AI day arrives. events.excerpt: ERC-3668 (CCIP-Read) lets a contract hand a read off to a gateway, but the gateway either has to be trusted or has to return a proof the contract can verify. For many cross-chain reads a valid proof cannot be produced. That does not make the read unsafe, because the client usually already trusts its own RPC connection to the other chain and could simply make the call itself. ERC-8446 lets the client act as the gateway. The contract reverts with OffchainLookup as usual, with an x-chain URL that names the chain and contract to read, and the client calls that contract with its own RPC and passes the result to the callback exactly as eth_call returns it. No third party is involved. events.excerpt: ERC-8048 and ERC-8049 store metadata onchain as key-value pairs, but a JSON document has no compact way to point at those values. A URL that names the contract, the chain, and the token ID repeats what the client already knows and differs for every token. ERC-8493 defines the onchain URI scheme. The contract and token ID are not written in the URI, they come from the function that returned the document. { "image": "onchain:image/png", "thumbnail": { "small": "onchain:image/png?key=thumb.small" } } onchain:image/png is 17 bytes and works unchanged for every token. When the URI comes from tokenURI or uri , the client reads it with metadata(tokenId, key) from ERC-8048, and when it comes from contractURI , with metadata(key) from ERC-8049. A direct member of the top-level document uses its own name as the key, and everywhere else the key parameter names it. Tokens that are already deployed can use the scheme by adding a metadata_contract property to their JSON, which points the client at a separate metadata contract. Linked JSON documents keep the same contract and token, so the whole thing reads as one data tree. The scheme adds no contract surface.
